scope: All 300 saved concept records, including the legacy Tonality record; 299 listed Dictionary concepts.
policy: Add only essential audible identification clues supported by saved notes; no new dates, composers or historical context.

MC-0001.addition: Blue notes are flattened or lowered notes that give the melody its characteristic blues colour.
MC-0001.supporting_excerpt: on a scale where some notes are flattened

MC-0106.addition: In a concerto, listen for the soloist playing alone or with little accompaniment, often finishing with a trill before the orchestra returns.

MC-0119.addition: It can also be plucked (pizzicato), producing short, detached bass notes instead of a sustained bowed line.

MC-0144.addition: Listen for a solo voice using operatic singing, usually supported by orchestral accompaniment.

MC-0163.addition: On voice, violin or trombone the slide can be smooth; on piano or harp, the individual pitches pass rapidly in succession.
MC-0163.supporting_excerpt: Some instruments can play a very smooth glissando

MC-0191.addition: It is often heard played on a plucked double bass, with a new bass note on each beat.
MC-0191.supporting_excerpt: often played on a double bass

MC-0213.addition: It can also be plucked (pizzicato), giving short, detached notes rather than a sustained bowed sound.

MC-0217.addition: The words are normally sung in German.

MC-0243.addition: A common example doubles the note values, so quavers become crotchets while the beat keeps the same speed.
MC-0243.supporting_excerpt: the length of the notes used are doubled

MC-0244.addition: A common example halves the note values, so crotchets become quavers while the beat keeps the same speed.
MC-0244.supporting_excerpt: the length of the notes used are halved

MC-0257.addition: Many of the rapid notes are sung on a single syllable, creating an extended melismatic run.
MC-0257.supporting_excerpt: a number of notes sung to the one syllable

MC-0261.addition: When two pitches alternate, they are normally at least a third apart, unlike the neighbouring notes of a trill.
MC-0261.supporting_excerpt: two different notes at least a 3rd apart

MC-0262.addition: The words are sung in English.

MC-0264.addition: Listen for the fa-la-la refrain returning at the end of each verse.
MC-0264.supporting_excerpt: at the end of each verse

MC-0265.addition: When sung, the hymn text is normally in German.

MC-0269.addition: Imitation is common: one voice begins a melodic idea and another copies it shortly afterwards.

MC-0272.addition: Listen for clear, balanced phrases and lighter textures combined with unexpectedly dissonant or atonal harmony.
MC-0272.supporting_excerpt: combined with dissonant, tonal and even atonal harmonies

MC-0284.addition: A usual turn sounds upper neighbour–main note–lower neighbour–main note; an inverted turn reverses this to lower neighbour–main note–upper neighbour–main note.
MC-0284.supporting_excerpt: the note above, the main note, the note below, and the main note again
